title: Buffon’s needle
objectives: Estimate $\pi$ from the chance that a dropped needle crosses a line.

screens.title: Drop a needle
screens.prose: A puzzle reported in bank final rounds. Needles of length 1 fall on a floor ruled with lines 1 apart. Each drop is two numbers: the angle $\theta$ to the lines, and the centre's distance to the nearest line. Drag the drop in the lower chart.

derive.caption: Angle {{round(P.x * 180 / pi)}}°, centre {{fixed(P.y, 2)}} from the nearest line: {{P.y <= 0.5 * sin(P.x) ? "it crosses" : "it misses"}}.

screens.question: When does the needle cross a line?

options.text: When the centre is closer to the line than $\tfrac12\sin\theta$
When the centre is closer to the line than $\tfrac12$
options.why: That is the half-length. A needle lying flat, at $\theta = 0$, never crosses wherever it lies.
A steep needle still misses if its centre sits mid-gap.

hints.text: The needle reaches $\tfrac12$ along itself from the centre.
Across the lines it reaches $\tfrac12\sin\theta$.
It crosses when the distance is below that reach.

feedback.correct: It crosses when the distance is below $\tfrac12\sin\theta$, under the curve.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the drop under and over the curve and watch the needle.

byKey.half: You used the half-length along the needle. Only its height across the lines matters, $\tfrac12\sin\theta$.

explain.text: Half the needle rises $\tfrac12\sin\theta$ across the lines. It crosses when the centre is nearer the line than that. In the lower chart that is the region under the curve.

screens.title: Count the area
screens.prose: The distance is uniform on $[0, \tfrac12]$ and the angle uniform on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$. So the drop is uniform in the rectangle, of area $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
screens.question: What is the chance the needle crosses a line? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Area under the curve over the area of the rectangle.
$\int_0^{\pi/2} \tfrac12\sin\theta\,d\theta = \tfrac12$.
$\tfrac12 \div \tfrac{\pi}4 = \tfrac2{\pi}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the area under the curve by the rectangle's area.

byKey.noscale: That is the area under the curve. Divide by the rectangle's $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
byKey.rect: That is the rectangle's area. The chance is the shaded share of it.

explain.text: The shaded area is $\tfrac12$ and the rectangle is $\tfrac{\pi}4$. So $P(\text{cross}) = \tfrac{2}{\pi}$. The $\pi$ comes from the angle's range.

screens.title: A shorter needle
screens.prose: Now the needle has length $\tfrac12$ on the same floor. The curve drops to $\tfrac14\sin\theta$.
screens.question: What is the chance it crosses? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The area under the curve halves.
It is $\tfrac14$.
$\tfrac14 \div \tfrac{\pi}4 = \tfrac1{\pi}$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac1{\pi} \approx 0.3183$: half the length, half the chance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The area under the curve is now $\tfrac14$.

byKey.old: That is the unit needle. The curve is half as tall now.
byKey.sq: You halved twice. The chance is linear in the length.

explain.text: Halving the needle halves the curve and the area under it. So the chance is $\tfrac1{\pi}$. For any $l \le 1$ it is $\tfrac{2l}{\pi}$.

screens.title: Estimate $\pi$
screens.prose: Turn it round: count crossings to estimate $\pi$. The engine's seeded run drops unit needles; its angle comes from a random point in a quarter disc, so no $\pi$ goes in.

state.caption: Points outside the quarter disc only set the angle, so they are discarded.

screens.question: In 10,000 drops, 6,366 needles cross. Estimate $\pi$ to four decimal places.

hints.text: $P(\text{cross}) = \tfrac2{\pi}$, so $\pi = \tfrac{2}{P}$.
Estimate $P$ by $\tfrac{6366}{10000}$.

byKey.no-two: You inverted the share but dropped the 2.
byKey.share: That is the share that crossed. Solve for $\pi$.

explain.text: The share crossing estimates $\tfrac2{\pi}$, so $\pi \approx 2 / 0.6366$. A run of 10,000 is typically off by about 0.024. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

screens.title: Two lines, or one?
screens.prose: A candidate sets it up differently. The angle is uniform on $[0, 2\pi)$. The centre's height above the line below is uniform on the whole gap $[0, 1]$. She tests only that line, with $y < \tfrac12|\sin\theta|$.
screens.question: What does her set-up give, and what is right?

options.text: Hers gives $\tfrac1{\pi}$; the answer is $\tfrac2{\pi}$, because a centre near the top crosses the line above

options.why: Testing only the line below misses every needle that crosses the line above. That halves the chance.

options.text: Doubling for the two lines, with distance on $[0, \tfrac12]$, gives $\tfrac4{\pi}$
options.why: That counts each crossing twice, and $\tfrac4{\pi}$ is above 1, so it cannot be a chance.

options.text: The wider angle range changes the answer
options.why: The angle range does not matter: $|\sin\theta|$ averages $\tfrac2{\pi}$ over any whole number of half-turns.

hints.text: Over the whole gap, which lines can a needle cross?
A centre near the top can cross the line above.
Counting one line halves the answer: $\tfrac1{\pi}$ instead of $\tfrac2{\pi}$.

feedback.correct: Hers gives $\tfrac1{\pi}$, half the truth, because she ignores the line above.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which lines a needle near the top of the gap can cross.

byKey.hers: You accepted one line on a whole gap. Either fold the distance to $[0, \tfrac12]$ or test both lines.

explain.text: Either use the nearest line, with distance on $[0, \tfrac12]$, or the whole gap and both lines. Mixing the two halves the answer or doubles it. Both clean set-ups give $\tfrac2{\pi}$.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Two random numbers, the angle and the distance, make a rectangle; the crossing is the region under a curve. For a needle of length $l$ on lines $d$ apart, with $l \le d$:

$$P(\text{cross}) = \frac{2l}{\pi d}.$$
screens.question: A needle of length 2 on lines 1 apart. Is its chance of crossing $\tfrac4{\pi}$?

options.text: No: $\tfrac4{\pi}$ is above 1; the formula needs $l \le d$, though $\tfrac{2l}{\pi d}$ still gives the expected number of crossings

options.why: The formula assumes at most one crossing. A long needle can cross two lines.

options.text: No: it is $\tfrac2{\pi}$, the same as length 1
options.why: A longer needle crosses more often. The chance is above $\tfrac2{\pi}$.

hints.text: A chance cannot exceed 1.
A long needle can cross two lines at once.
The formula then counts crossings, not drops that cross.

feedback.correct: Right: past $l = d$ the formula gives expected crossings, not a chance.

explain.text: When $l > d$ one needle can cross two lines, so the chance formula changes. The expected number of crossings is still $\tfrac{2l}{\pi d}$, by linearity. Here that is $\tfrac4{\pi} \approx 1.27$.

screens.title: The general needle
screens.prose: Lines 1 apart, a needle of length $l \le 1$. The curve is $\tfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta$ over the same rectangle of area $\tfrac{\pi}4$.
screens.question: Write $P(\text{cross})$ in terms of $l$.

hints.text: The area under $\tfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta$ from 0 to $\tfrac{\pi}2$ is $\tfrac{l}{2}$.
Divide by $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$\tfrac{l}{2} \cdot \tfrac4{\pi} = \tfrac{2l}{\pi}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the area under the curve by $\tfrac{\pi}4$.

byKey.no-two: That halves it, as testing one line on the whole gap does.
byKey.four: That doubles it, as if each crossing were counted twice.

explain.text: The area under the curve is $\tfrac{l}{2}$, and the rectangle is $\tfrac{\pi}4$. Their ratio is $\tfrac{2l}{\pi}$, linear in $l$.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `buffon_estimate(drops, length, gap, seed)` for `length <= gap`. Use `random.Random(seed)`, count crossings, and return the estimate of $\pi$. Drawing the angle uses `math.pi`; the point is to watch the estimate converge.
screens.question: Write the estimator.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 4 accept an estimate within three standard errors of $\pi$ over 100,000 drops. Test 5 runs one seed twice.

hints.text: Draw the distance on `[0, gap / 2]` and the angle on `[0, math.pi / 2]`.
A drop crosses when `distance <= length / 2 * math.sin(angle)`.
The share crossing estimates `2 * length / (math.pi * gap)`; solve for pi.

feedback.correct: The estimates land within the noise of $\pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: The estimate is far from $\pi$. Check the distance runs to `gap / 2` and the angle to `math.pi / 2`.
byKey.test-3: The gap is 2 here. Put `gap` in both the distance range and the final formula.

explain.text: The model solution gives 3.1399 with seed 1 and 100,000 drops. One drop is a 0 or a 1, so the estimate's standard error is about 0.0075. A digit more needs a hundred times the drops.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all; keep your own time. Lines are 1 apart. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: A needle of length $\tfrac13$: chance it crosses
A needle of length 2: expected number of lines it crosses
A unit needle on a square grid, lines 1 apart both ways: chance it crosses at least one

hints.text: Short needle: $\tfrac{2l}{\pi}$.
Long needle: split it into two unit needles and add their expected crossings.
Square grid: $\tfrac{4l - l^2}{\pi}$ with $l = 1$, which is $\tfrac3{\pi}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: Check: two unit needles, $\tfrac2{\pi}$ expected crossings each.

explain.text: The short needle scales: $\tfrac{2}{3\pi}$. Expected crossings add over pieces, so length 2 gives $\tfrac4{\pi}$. On a square grid the unit needle crosses some line with chance $\tfrac3{\pi} \approx 0.95$.

screens.title: Follow-up: a bent needle
screens.prose: You gave $\tfrac2{\pi}$. The interviewer asks about a noodle: any rigid curve of length $L$ crosses $\tfrac{2L}{\pi d}$ lines on average, by linearity over tiny pieces. Take a wire circle of diameter 1 on lines 1 apart.
screens.question: How many crossings does the circle make on average?

hints.text: The circle's length is $L = \pi$.
$\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi \times 1} = 2$.
Check: a circle of diameter 1 always meets exactly one line, in two points.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $L = \pi$ and $d = 1$ into $\tfrac{2L}{\pi d}$.

byKey.one: It meets one line, but in two points. Crossings count points.
byKey.chance: That is a straight unit needle. The circle is longer, $L = \pi$.

explain.text: The circle has length $\pi$, so it averages $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2$ crossings. In fact it makes exactly 2 every time. The circle is one way to prove Buffon: it fixes the constant.

screens.title: The price of a digit
screens.prose: A desk prices a payoff with no formula by Monte Carlo. Like Buffon, its error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$. Our unit needle's estimate of $\pi$ has a standard error of about 0.024 with 10,000 drops.
screens.question: How many drops give a standard error of about 0.0024?

hints.text: The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.
A tenth of the error needs $10^2$ times the drops.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dividing the error by 10 multiplies $n$ by $10^2$.

byKey.ten: You multiplied by 10. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so you need $10^2$.

explain.text: One more digit costs a hundred times the work. That is why desks use variance reduction and closed forms where they can. Buffon is the cleanest picture of the cost.

ideas: A drop is two uniform numbers, angle and distance: a rectangle where area is chance.
The needle crosses under the curve $\tfrac{l}{2}\sin\theta$, so $P = \tfrac{2l}{\pi d}$ for $l \le d$.
Counting crossings estimates $\pi$, with an error that shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

formula.name: Buffon's needle
formula.note: Expected crossings are $\tfrac{2L}{\pi d}$ for any curve of length $L$.

summary.trap: Mixing set-ups: the whole gap with one line halves the answer; half the gap with both lines doubles it.

quiz.prose: A unit needle falls on lines 2 apart.
quiz.question: What is the chance it crosses a line? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\tfrac{2l}{\pi d}$ with $d = 2$.

byKey.unit: That is for lines 1 apart. Wider gaps mean fewer crossings.

explain.text: Doubling the gap halves the chance: $\tfrac{2l}{\pi d} = \tfrac1{\pi}$.

quiz.prose: A needle of length 3 falls on lines 1 apart.
quiz.question: What is the expected number of lines it crosses? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split it into three unit needles.

byKey.unit: That is one unit needle. Add three.
byKey.capped: That caps it at one crossing. A long needle can cross several lines.

explain.text: Expected crossings add over pieces, so three unit needles give $\tfrac6{\pi}$. Linearity holds even though the pieces move together.

quiz.prose: A Buffon estimate of $\pi$ from 10,000 drops is too noisy.
quiz.question: How many drops halve its standard error?

options.why: Doubling the drops cuts the error by $\sqrt2$ only.

feedback.correct: Four times the drops halves the error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

explain.text: Halving $1/\sqrt{n}$ needs $n$ four times larger. So 40,000 drops.
